CS 6672 · hacker presentation

GhostMap

What can the surviving world prove about a building that no longer exists?

COLMAP, extended with things the world already knows: measured lidar ground, the camera's own EXIF focal length, and people.

Cornell Arts Quad · Boardman Hall (built 1892, demolished 1959; Olin Library stands on its site) · public-domain and Creative Commons photographs only, no annotation.

The problem

A vanished building, seen only in old postcards

  • About 24 public-domain photographs of Boardman Hall exist online (1898–1934), almost all postcards from the same side.
  • Unknown camera, unknown focal length, cropped, hand-coloured.
  • The building is gone, so the only geometry that can place these photographs is the buildings that survived: McGraw Tower and Uris Library.
  • Classic question: can we recover Boardman? Better question: what does the surviving record determine, and what does it not?
1934 postcard, Boardman Hall and the library. Public domain, Wikimedia Commons.
Stock COLMAP · Extension 1

Fragments, no scale, focal lengths that blow up

Mapping (the 145-photo snapshot has 77 training photographs)cameras per modelregisteredfocal ratio outside 0.5–3

Extension 1, EXIF-anchored calibration: photographs whose EXIF gives the focal length keep it fixed (constant_cameras); the rest are bounded.

Focal blow-ups mostly vanish, but the fragments do not merge. Missing views, not calibration, split the scene.
Extension 2

Snap COLMAP to the measured world

Public-domain USGS airborne lidar ( points) and OpenStreetMap footprints. No geotags, no hand-picked points.

  • Vertical from facade normals (camera "up" is biased 15° by people tilting up at the tower).
  • Scale from photographers standing on the ground vs the measured tower top: m/unit.
  • Independent scale from the library's walls: m/unit → apart.
  • Library points on library walls: median m.
The hidden ambiguity

COLMAP doesn't know where its own photographers stood

Bundle adjustment places modern photographers well off the measured ground, some 30–50 m in the air, with sub-2-pixel error.

Why: a distant camera can slide along its viewing ray while the focal length changes (the dolly-zoom ambiguity). Re-solving each one from just the tower and the library next to it:

m → m

Median 95 % interval along the viewing ray, anchors only → plus "the photographer stood on the measured ground".

Extension 3

The surviving world as a calibration target

Each postcard: for every focal length, COLMAP's pose solver places the camera through surviving anchors. The cost over all anchors is a likelihood along the ambiguity ray; extra cues reweight it.

Photographanchors only+ measured ground+ people

Width of the 95 % interval of the photographer's position along the viewing ray.

People as cross-century anchors

1914: sixteen people pin the camera to 7 m

Pedestrians stand on today's measured ground and are about 1.70 m tall, at many depths — exactly the depth spread that breaks the dolly-zoom ambiguity.

m → m → m

anchors only → + measured ground → + people

Check the fit never used: at the best pose the people's implied heights have median m.

In the spirit of Virtual Correspondence (humans as geometry where surfaces don't overlap), but linking one photo to a measured ground across a century.

What fooled it

Every Boardman pose is a mirror image

  • All 22 modern photographers in the fragment stand west or south-west of the tower, so the model only has its west and south faces.
  • The postcards were taken from the Arts Quad, north-east of the site.
  • McGraw Tower looks alike from every side: east-face features matched west-face points. The pose fits every anchor and even faces the Boardman site — from the wrong side.
Found by checking left–right order against the map, not by the pipeline. Confirmed on the 228-photo snapshot: all 26 tower photographers again stand west or south-west. No bound on Boardman is shown; the fix is data from the Quad side.

Honest limits · next

What we can and cannot claim

  • Can: COLMAP extended with EXIF focal priors, a lidar anchor and a measured-ground prior; certificates that say how far along its ray each photograph is undetermined; people as a cue.
  • Cannot (yet): any geometry of Boardman Hall. Every registered pose is mirrored; the frame's two scales differ by 5.4 %; principal point and lens distortion are not modelled.
  • Next: photographs of the tower from the Arts Quad side (the 228-photo snapshot still has none); an automatic handedness check; carving a 2.5-D bound once poses are right (implemented, tested on synthetic data); calibrating certificates on simulated demolition.
